summary: First Contact.sys helps mission designers, researchers, and students explore where and when a lunar lander can survive and operate. Grounded in published NASA LOLA topography and JPL DE421 ephemeris, our browser observatory evaluates 14 south-polar candidate locations. Users interactively compare landing dispersion offsets, 30-day arrival windows, and observer mast heights to inspect solar illumination, Earth line-of-sight, and modeled battery reserves. Recent CLPS missions like Athena demonstrate that reaching the surface is only the first hurdle. First Contact.sys bridges immersive 3D exploration with high-speed WebAssembly scenario screening, trade-off comparisons, and downloadable data, making early lunar planning accessible while keeping scientific assumptions and limitations completely transparent.
details:
1. The Operational Challenge: Beyond the Touchdown

We built First Contact.sys around what happens after touchdown. A lunar spacecraft needs enough sunlight to generate power, sufficient stored energy to survive periods of darkness, and regular opportunities to communicate with Earth. At the lunar south pole, where the Sun skims low across the terrain, these conditions are governed by the surrounding ridges and crater rims just as much as nominal coordinates and landing dates.

Recent commercial missions illustrate how decisively surface topography shapes operations:

  • IM-2 Athena (March 2025): Landed on its side inside a crater near Mons Mouton; NASA reported that its orientation prevented solar recharging, bringing surface operations to an early close. NASA's account of IM-2
  • IM-1 Odysseus (February 2024): Landed off-vertical, creating communications and operational challenges, yet completed seven days of instrument operations to meet its primary objectives. NASA's account of IM-1

We treat these missions as vital case studies in operating under unexpected local conditions, rather than simple pass/fail outcomes.

2. The Observatory Experience & Capabilities

First Contact.sys makes these geometry, illumination, and power questions accessible through an interactive browser observatory:

  • 3D Terrain & Horizon Visualization: Users inspect the landing terrain alongside a 360-degree skyline horizon mask that tracks the Sun and Earth across the lunar sky.
  • Calculated Operational Metrics: The platform models continuous illumination, simultaneous Sun-and-Earth visibility, maximum continuous darkness, and battery state-of-charge over time.
  • Landing Dispersion Grid (5×5): Users can test 25 discrete touchdown offsets across a 500m × 500m footprint to see how shifting 100 meters alters local slope stability and line-of-sight blockage.
  • 30-Day Launch-Slip Scan: Evaluates whether adjusting the arrival date opens a longer, more resilient operating window.
  • Dynamic Mast Clearance: Evaluates how raising an antenna or solar mast (from 0.5m to 10m) lowers the effective horizon obstacle angle, helping clear nearby ridges.

3. NASA Data & Geometric Pipeline

  • Topography: 14 candidate landing locations derived from published NASA LOLA Digital Elevation Models (5 to 60 meters per pixel, sourced from NASA GSFC PGDA Products 78, 90, and 104).
  • Ephemeris: 2,185 hourly topocentric Sun and Earth vectors per site generated from JPL DE421 ephemeris and NAIF SPICE kernels.
  • Calibration Plane: A synthetic flat-plane case is included to verify code invariants and baseline geometry; it is explicitly excluded from real-site recommendations.
  • Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs): Mapped PSRs provide geographical context; proximity is strictly reported as geographic distance, not confirmed water ice.

4. Technical Architecture

  • Frontend: Built with React 19, TypeScript, and Three.js for responsive orbital, terrain, and horizon rendering.
  • Analytical Engine: A high-performance Rust engine compiled to WebAssembly (WASM) executes multi-variable searches across 4,500 combinations of positions, arrival dates, and heights in the browser.
  • Offline Pipeline: Python, Rasterio, and SPICE handle offline data ingest, DEM windowing, and atomic payload verification.
  • Open Evidence: Users can export calculated results as CSVs for external verification and trade-space analysis.

5. The Philosophy of Contact

The project draws its name and visual identity from the dual meaning of "contact." In lunar exploration, touching down on the regolith is only half the equation; the decisive contact is telecommunication... the fragile, unbroken line-of-sight linking the explorer back to Earth.

Our logo and artwork draw subtle foreshadowing from Michelangelo’s The Creation of Adam, depicting two hands reaching across the dark void, separated by an agonizingly narrow gap before touch is made. In polar lunar exploration, mission survival hinges on that exact gap. A ridge 20 kilometers away can sever communications and freeze power, while an antenna raised by two meters or a touchdown shifted by 100 meters reaches across the skyline to close the circuit and bridge the silence. First Contact.sys was built to make that delicate, life-sustaining margin visible and understandable.

6. Intended Impact & Scientific Boundaries

Our objective is to make preliminary lunar trade studies transparent and interactive for students, researchers, and mission concept teams. In keeping with scientific integrity:

  • We have not reconstructed the exact telemetry or failure causes of Athena or Odysseus, and make no claim our tool would have prevented them.
  • Spacecraft power profiles and thermal limits are illustrative engineering assumptions.
  • Geometric Earth line-of-sight is a necessary geometric condition, not a certified Deep Space Network (DSN) link budget or flight readiness sign-off.
